narrationScript: A crucial concept in CSS for controlling layout and spacing is the **box model**. The browser treats every HTML element on a webpage as a rectangular box. This box isn't just the content you see; it's composed of four distinct layers, working from the inside out. At the very center is the **content** itself—your text, images, or other elements. Surrounding the content is **padding**, which provides internal space between the content and the element's border. Think of it as cushioning. Next, we have the **border**, a visible line that wraps around both the content and its padding. This border can have various styles, widths, and colors. Finally, on the outermost layer, is the **margin**. This creates external space around the entire element, separating it from other elements on the page. Understanding these components is vital because `width` and `height` properties typically refer only to the content area. Padding, border, and margin are *added* on top of that, which can sometimes lead to unexpected element sizes. A common solution to this is `box-sizing: border-box;`, which alters the calculation so that `width` and `height` include the padding and border. Mastering the box model will help you precisely control the layout and spacing of all elements on your web pages.
deliveryNotes: Explain each layer of the box model clearly.
Emphasize the default calculation of width/height.
